source.title: The Dragon Hatchling: The Missing Link between the Transformer and Models of the Brain
source.how_accessed: Public abstract, Semantic Scholar summary, and Pathway public communications (pathway.com). We did not have offline access to the full paper PDF at submission time.
source.citation_note: Every claim below is attributed to the abstract, introduction, or publicly available summary of arXiv:2509.26507. We quote or closely paraphrase the source. We do NOT reproduce the full paper text.

WHY_NO_SPECIFIC_NUMBERS.explanation: Specific quantitative benchmark results (e.g., exact perplexity on WikiText-103, exact accuracy on a named benchmark at a named parameter scale) from the paper are NOT included in this file. We had access to public summaries that describe performance qualitatively ('rivals GPT-2 performance') but not to specific table entries with enough precision to cite responsibly. Fabricating or guessing specific figures would be worse than omitting them. A future contributor with access to the full paper PDF should populate the 'quantitative_claims' section below.

qualitative_claims.claim: BDH achieves Transformer-like performance on language and translation tasks at equivalent parameter scales.
qualitative_claims.paraphrase: The paper claims BDH 'rivals GPT-2 performance' on language modeling and translation tasks at parameter counts from 10M to 1B.
qualitative_claims.source_quote: Described in the abstract and Pathway public communications as achieving 'Transformer-like performance' and 'rival[ing] GPT-2'.

qualitative_claims.claim: BDH uses a fixed-size synaptic/Hebbian memory rather than a growing KV cache.
qualitative_claims.paraphrase: BDH's working memory is based on synaptic plasticity and Hebbian learning with spiking neurons. Memory size is bounded and does not grow with context length.
qualitative_claims.source_quote: The paper describes 'working memory based on synaptic plasticity and Hebbian learning with spiking neurons' as a core architectural feature.

qualitative_claims.claim: BDH offers inherent interpretability through sparse, monosemantic features.
qualitative_claims.paraphrase: The model exhibits sparse, positive activation vectors. Specific synapses strengthen when the model processes specific concepts, enabling feature-level inspection without post-hoc probing methods.
qualitative_claims.source_quote: The paper claims 'inherent interpretability' arising from 'sparse, positive activation vectors' and 'monosemantic features (specific synapses strengthen when processing specific concepts)'.
qualitative_claims.source: arXiv:2509.26507 (via Semantic Scholar summary and daily.dev summary)

qualitative_claims.claim: BDH is GPU-friendly despite being conceptually a graph-based model.
qualitative_claims.paraphrase: Although BDH is architecturally a scale-free graph of locally interacting neuron particles, the paper demonstrates a GPU-friendly formulation allowing efficient scaling on standard hardware.
qualitative_claims.source_quote: Authors demonstrate 'a GPU-friendly formulation' of the graph-based architecture.

qualitative_claims.claim: BDH targets the problem of generalization over time as a path toward universal reasoning.
qualitative_claims.paraphrase: The authors identify the inability to generalize over time as 'a primary barrier to universal reasoning in AI' and position BDH as a step toward solving it through dynamic synaptic updates.
qualitative_claims.source_quote: Pathway positions BDH as addressing 'generalisation over time' as 'a primary barrier to achieving universal reasoning'.

our_toy_layer_vs_bdh.summary: Our bdh_inspired_state.py is a toy layer inspired by BDH's concept, NOT a reimplementation.
our_toy_layer_vs_bdh.shared_concept: Both use a fixed-size state that overwrites (rather than appends), so memory is O(state_size) independent of sequence length. This is the conceptual insight we demonstrate in the UI.
our_simplifications_vs_real_bdh: We use a flat slot array M[n_heads, state_size, d_head] instead of a scale-free graph topology.
Our write rule is a hand-designed soft outer-product write (EMA + softmax addressing). Real BDH uses learned synaptic update rules with spiking neuron dynamics.
We use a fixed scalar decay parameter. Real BDH has per-synapse learned plasticity.
We do not implement BDH's 'neuron particle' abstraction at all.
Our implementation has NO trained weights. BDH is a full trained model.
